Funeral of Col. Frank A, Brown.
At 2 o’clock, yesterday afternoon, a large
cconcourse of people assembled at the Unitar
ian Church, at the corner of Merrimack and
Pine streets, to witness the funeral ceremon
jes of Col. Frank A. Brown. A large part
of the body of the house had been reserved
for the accommodation of the mourners, Uity
Officials and Odd Fellows.
When the procession arrived at the church
and upon entering, so poignant and heart
rending was the feelings and grief of Mrs.
B. that she nearly fainted, and was borne to
her appropriate seat by the pastor and one
of the relatives of the deceased. It was a very
sad and affecting sight, and not a dry eye
could be seen in the vast assembly. i
His Honor the Mayor, the Aldermen, City}
Clerk and Common Council, came in and
took their seats upon one side of the body of
the house, while the Odd Fellows, with some
of their insignia of office, trimmed with black
crape, occupied the other. Other citizens
and ladies filled the remainder of the build
ing to overflowing, many being obliged to
stand during the entire exercises.
The Rev. Mr. Hunting, pastor of the Uni
tarian Society officiated, and commenced the
services by reading some passages from the
22d chapter of Matthew, and the 15th chap
ter of Ist Corinthians.
The Choir then very impressively sang the
509th Hymn of the Collection, used by the
Unitarian Society, commencing thus
«How blest the righteous when he dies
When sinks a weary soul to rest.”
The Rev. Mr. Hunting then-arose and an
nounced as the foundation of his remarks,
upon this sad and solemn occasion the follow
ing text:
Jeremiah 48th, 17th—and Luke 11th, 10th. All ye that
are about him, bemoan him and all ye that know his
pame, say, How is the strong staff broken, and the beau
tiful rod
Friend, go up higher.
The Rev. Speaker said he knew of no oth
er words that better expressed the sentiment,
that seemed to be on every tongue of him
wh» rightly knew this friend, than those of
the text. How is the strong staff broken,and
the beautiful rod! The staff and the rod,
were emblems of strength -and power, and
becaure we felt that some of that strength
was gone, on which we depended, and the
power that so gratified us, had fallen, we
moaned.
A short week since we heard the news of
the severe sickness of our brother. Each one
of us felt that we must do something, if pcs
sible, and we all asked what we coulddo?
Not for one moment could we endure the
thought that his sickness was unto death.
When we met, we said that we could not
give up Frank Brown now and we comfort
ed ourselves with the least shadow of hope
that came to us.
We who had learned to love him, said that
we would give our right hand to save him,
if that would do it. But it was not so to
be. He returned to the mother who bore
him, to permit her trembling hand to per
form the last office of love, as when in the
full strength of womanhood, they first clasp
ed the new born son to her bosom; and he
laid down his body to moulder back to its
mother earth, while he goes ‘‘up higher.”
The sad word comes at length ,when we were
too little prepared for it. 'We know that the
Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away,
but we find it very difficult to say in refer
ence to this last act, *“blessed be the name of
the Lord.”” We pray that we all may have
the religious resignation to say, ‘“Thy will
be done.”’
We see by the shock that we have received
by this event, how much the life of one man
who makes no pretension of scholarship or
learning, who seemed to me always so un
pretending in everything, runsinto, and min
gles with, the life of others. As the great
truth which is here taught us that we are all
one family that the gracious Father has
wisely linked together the hearts of his chil
dren by golden sympathies, and only when
some sudden providence breaks up the deep
fountains of the better life within the soul,
do we feel the sacredness of the tie that binds
us all together.
One man, not of our religious society, said
to me when the news of his death came, that
we ‘“‘could better loose a regiment of com
mon men.”’ This was indeed, the language
of the heart, but it may be true for the in
tellect also.
From some cause or other, our friend had
become a strong staff’ and a ‘beautiful rod’
to many persons, who, until the fact of his
departure from earth, did not wholly realize
it. And it was because, in the very best
sense of the phrase, he was a common man,
that we all feel theloss. To some of you he
was more than the household gods of the an
eients, whose image was regarded as a sure
defence against harm.
Is there any one, who knew him asa friend,
who is capable of the exercise of the finer
emotions, that will not say he loved him
The scene that the Evangelist has given of
Jesus weeping at the grave of Lazarus, when
the Jews that looked on,said, Behold, how
he Joved him,’’ is made new and real to the
hearts of many of us.
As great as we may feel the loss to be, there
is still another side to the picture. The loss
is only relative loss to us is gain to him,
and shall we not all pray that we may be
able from the heart to say, Friend, go up
higher.”
Dr. Bushnell calls man a careering force,
started on its way to eterngy ;-a principle of
mi%l;t and majesty begun to be unfolde<£ and
to be progressively unfolded forever. Intelli
gence, reason, conscience, observation, choice,
memory, enthusiasm, all the fires of his un
born eternity are kindling to a glow, and,
looking on him as a force immortal, just be
ginning to reveal the symptoms' of what he
shall be, we call him man. Only a few years
ago he lay in his cradle, a barely breathing
principle of life, but in that life were gath
ered up, as in a germ or seed, all these god
like powers that-are now so conspicuous in
the volume cf his personal growth. In a
sense, all that is in him now was in him then,
as the power of an endless life, and still the
sublime progression of his power is. only be
n."
sn'l‘he speaker here ?vo a brief sketch of the
elements which went to make u true’m-.‘
hood, which, he said bolummdpbo be devel
-oped from the elements of that nature which
as divine as that of which it is the image

elements moulded and nurtured by truth
and love till they appear in the form of char
acter. 'To have an instance of true manhood
it is not necessary to have a perfect man, but
a {rue man is wanted. A man, who, in the
general elements of his character and quali
ties of his life, will represent these that have
now been delineated.
His intellectual faculties, said the speaker,
appeared to be remarkably well balanced.—
His understanding was formed by much ob
servation of men and things, more than by
the study of books, which gave him more
than the usual degree of practical good sense.
But yet, he was not a cold utilitaran, and
never tired you with details of business.—
His imagination was too warm, and exerted
too much influence upon his thoughts to make
him ever uncongenial. His imagination pho
tographed pictures for his understanding
which was the gallery in which he hung
them. His power of observation was re
markable, which, with his good taste, gave
him the ability to succeed as an artist. His
judgment you will often seek for in vain, for
his decisions must always have had weight
with his friends.
But the characteristics that most attracted
his friends, range higher still. As a man of
strict moral integrity, of unswerving recti
tude a man of conscience —he won our
unqualified confidence. Benevolence mel
lowed all his virtues, acd he judged of his
duty to give away his money more by the
wants of the sufferer —the cause to be aided
than by his own pecuniary means. Did
an unfortunate neighbor or relative need his
aid, his hand was open and his heart gener
ous. In will, intellect, and heart, he was
alive, and this made him the public-spirited
citizen that he was.
His was that cheerful spirit, which in the
social circle always creates free, manly com
panionship, and forgets the false distinctions
of a rank, pretension, or obscurity,and finds
something good in all, and awakens self-re
spect and confidence in the minds of the dis
trusting and desponding.
His heart gave the character to his religious
opinions, for he could not believe a stern and
cold creed. He was positive in his convictions
and liberal in his fellowship. Ie could not
be a pharisee to save his life; and to feign
worship when he felt it not, would be impos
sible. He prayed with his kear¢ and hands
more than with his Zps. His presence ¥arm
ed me while his thought enlightened. He
asked for free and liberal expressions of truth,
and demanded freedom as the soul’s preroga
tive. He is to us then, not an unworthy ex
ample of true manhood.
The speaker here eloquently spoke of the
faithfulness and fidelity of the deceased to
his home, his friends, and all those bound to
him by love and nature, and said, such is the
tribute that my soul gives to our brother. I
speak as a friend, and brother, but with com
plete sincerity, when I say, try him by the
heart, and he is gold weigh him by the in
tellect, and he is still pure coin, bearing the
image of righteousness, and the superscrip
tion, fidelity to all men.”’
While, then, we all feel our /loss, let us
think, also, of the gain of his life, and let us
prove the sincerity of our_tears by embalming
his virtues. All that is generous and brave,
noble and good, that we have known in his
life on earth,should be treasured up in sacred
remembrance, to be an example for ourselves
and others, in the coming time.
As a legislator and councilor, has he thrown
his influence for temperance, for a high-toned
morality in the community has his heart
beat warm at the demands of the poor and
the oppressed the best expression of our re
gard for him will be seen in our hearty en
deavors to carry on the work that he has
helped sustain. Having passed the bourn,
we will not wish him back though the
strong staff be broken, and the beautiful
rod!’’ but will think of his virtues and his
strong, sympathizing heart we will live on
the remembrance of his good deeds, thankful
that the benediction of his love has always
rested like the sweet dew of heaven upon his
wife, his brothers and sisters and that to us
his friendship has been a continual source of
moral strength and we will say, Brother,
Friend, go up higher —go up higher!
Here a few affectionate and appropriate re
marks were addressed, by the speaker, to the
mourning friends, when he closed with the
following very beautiful selection of poetry
Not tn the grave, not to the grave, my soul,
_ Follow thy friend beloved
But in the lonely hour,
But in the evening shade,
Think that he ’companies thy solitude.”
With si/ence only as their benediction,
God’s angels come,
‘When, in the shadow of a great affliction,
The soul sits dumb
Yet, would 1 say, what my own heart approveth
Our Father’s will,
Calling to him the dear one whom he loveth,
Is mercy still— v
Not upon thee or thine, the solemn angel
Hath evil wrought
His funeral anthem is a glad evangel,
The good die not!
God calls our loved ones, but we loose not whslly,
‘What he hath given
They live on earth in thought ana deed, as truly
As in his heaven—
And ke is with thee in thy path of trial,
He walketh yet,
Still with the Baptism of thy self-denial
His locks are wet.”
A hymn was now sung by the choir, when
the Rev. Mr. Pierce of the First Baptist
Church, on invitation from the pastor, made
a very touching and excellent J)rayer, after
which Mr. Hunting pronounced the benedic
tion, and the long procession was again form
ed and escorted tge mourners and friends to
the late residence of the deceased, he having
been buried on first arriving in the city, from
Groton, where he died, it being found upon
examination, that it would be impossible to
keep the corpse any longer.
Thus has passed one of the saddest events
that it has been our misfortune to ever wit
ness in Manchester. "We would say that we
have been unpable to give but a meagre and
brief abstract of the excellent and eloquent
discourse delivered upon this occasion. We
would have been glad tojhave given the whole,
but want of space forbids.
Burns CELEBRATION IN Pilscaraquoc.—The
Scoteh of this city held a private celebration
of the birthday of Robert Burns, on the 25th
ult. The Secretary sends us a report which
would have been published in full, had it
been furnished us at the time. About sixty
in number assembled at the Merrimack House
in Piscataquog, and after dancing till 11
o’clock in the Hall, (which was decorated
with evergreens, portraits of Burns, Wash
ington, “John Anderson, my Joe, John,”
&0.,) they sat down to a supper prepared in
style by Mr. Turney. Three Scotch Haggis
ses graced the table, and Mr. James M. Gar-%
ret gave, in Scotch dialect, Burns’ address to
the Haggiss,and then asked a blessing accord
ing to custom. Songs, sentiments, speeches,i
Highland Flings, &c. &c., rendered it an
evening of much pleasure.

The man with the Sugar-Loaf Hat has
been here the past two or three days astonish
ing the natives with the wonderful effects
produced by DE GRATH’S ELECTRIC OIL.
Prof. De Grath has invented a novel mode
of advertising. He makes his adventin town
by ringing a tremendous gong, which attracts
the attention of the crowd, to whom he
makes known the wonderful virtues of his
Electric Oil, and begs them to send all who
are suffering rheumatism, pains of all kinds,
and deafness, to the Town Hall, where he
has lectured mornings and evenings, for sev
eral days, and produced sowe astonishin
curcs. A Mr. Sugg and Seth Taylor, who
have been long aftected with chronic rheu
matism, and bhad wo be assisted on the stage,
were enabled to run a race across the hall
and up and down stairs, to the amusement
of the audience. A number of cases, of ma
ny years standing, were relieved in five or
ten minutes, so they eould hear the ticking
of a watch, and evinced their gratitude by
embracing the Professor, and showering up
on him their endless blessings. Some cases
were truly affecting.
Prof. De Grath has been called to see a
number of obstinate cases in our most respec
table families, and has succeeded in affor
ding great relief and a number have given
him certificates which will be published
soon. He makes no charge, but directs all
who want De Grath’s Electric Oil, to Pescud
Gatling who have purchased a large quaun
ity on such terms as will enable them to sup
ply the country merchants at his price. This
valuable preparation is selling rapidly.
A number of valuable presents have been
made to the Professor by those who have
been relieved.
